module_title: Building a Quality Management System for Export

lessons.title: Writing a simple quality manual
lessons.body: A quality manual is the rulebook for how your business makes consistent products. It doesn't need to be long. For a small African exporter, 10 to 15 pages is plenty. Start with a one-page cover: your company name, what you make, and a promise to meet customer and legal requirements. Then add sections for each key process: buying raw materials, production, packing, storage, and shipping. For each process, write what you do, who does it, and what records you keep. For example, under 'Buying Raw Materials', you might write: 'We buy from approved suppliers only. We check every delivery against a written spec. We record the supplier name, date, and result in a Goods Received Log.' Use simple language. Write in English or your local language, but if you export, English is safer. You can download free templates from ISO.org or from the African Organisation for Standardisation (ARSO). But don't just copyâadapt to your reality. If you don't have a machine, don't write about it. Number each section (1.0, 2.0, etc.) so you can refer to them in training and audits. Include a simple process map: a flowchart showing how a raw material becomes a finished export product. This helps new staff understand the big picture. Keep the manual in a binder or as a PDF on a shared phone or computer. Review it every year or when something changes. A quality manual is not for show; it's for daily use. In Kenya, a small honey exporter used a 12-page manual to get HACCP certification. In Ghana, a shea butter cooperative used a 10-page manual to satisfy a European buyer. You can do the same.

lessons.title: Document control for small teams
lessons.body: Document control means making sure everyone uses the same, latest version of every document. Without it, you might use an old recipe while your colleague uses a new one, leading to inconsistent quality. For a small team, keep it simple. First, list all documents you need: quality manual, work instructions, forms (like batch records), and external documents (like buyer specs). Give each a unique code: QM-01 for quality manual, WI-01 for work instruction, FR-01 for form. Add a version number and date: 'Version 2, 01/03/2025'. Create a master listâa single sheet of paper or a spreadsheetâshowing every document, its code, version, and where the original is kept. Designate one person as document controller, even if part-time. Their job: when a document changes, they update the master list, print new copies, and collect old ones. Stamp old copies 'OBSOLETE' and keep one for records. For digital files, use a shared folder on Google Drive or a USB stick. Name files clearly: 'WI-01_Packing_Instructions_v2_2025-03-01.pdf'. Train everyone on how to find the current version. At the start of each shift, they should check the master list or the shared folder. If you use paper, keep binders at each workstation. When a document is updated, replace the page and note the change. For records like batch sheets, number them sequentially and store them for at least 3 years (or as buyer requires). In Ethiopia, a coffee exporter uses a simple logbook to track document changes. In Nigeria, a food processor uses colour-coded folders: green for current, red for obsolete. This prevents costly mistakes.

lessons.title: Training your staff on standards
lessons.body: Training is how you turn written standards into daily habits. You don't need a classroom. Start with a training matrix: a table listing every staff member and the skills they need. For example, a packer needs to know hygiene rules, correct labelling, and how to fill a batch record. A machine operator needs to know cleaning and safety. Identify who needs what. Then plan short sessionsâ30 minutes once a week works well. Use the quality manual and work instructions as your textbook. Demonstrate the task, then let the staff do it while you watch. Ask them to explain back to you why it matters. For example, show a packer how to check a label for the correct batch number and expiry date. Then have them check 10 labels and tell you what they found. Keep a training record: date, topic, trainer, attendees, and a simple test or observation result. This record is proof for auditors. Use local examples: if you export mangoes, talk about a rejected shipment due to wrong temperature. If you make shea butter, talk about a buyer complaint about rancid smell. Make it real. For low-literacy staff, use pictures and symbols. Create a one-page visual guide for each critical step. Post it at the workstation. In Tanzania, a cashew processor uses Swahili posters showing correct moisture testing. In Senegal, a fish processor uses a buddy system: new staff shadow experienced ones for two weeks. Retrain whenever a process changes or a mistake happens. Celebrate good performanceâa small bonus or public recognition goes a long way. Training is not a one-time event; it's ongoing.

lessons.title: Internal audits: doing them yourself
lessons.body: An internal audit is a check-up on your own quality system. You do it to find problems before a buyer or certifier does. Plan to audit each part of your system at least once a year. If you're small, you can do one audit per month covering one area, e.g., January: purchasing, February: production, March: packing. You don't need an outside expert. Train one or two staff as internal auditorsâthey should not audit their own work. Use a simple checklist based on your quality manual. For each requirement, ask: Do we have a written procedure? Are we following it? Show me the record. For example, check if raw material deliveries are inspected. Look at the Goods Received Log. Are all entries complete? If not, that's a finding. Write findings in a report: what you checked, what you found, and whether it's a major or minor issue. A major issue is something that could cause a unsafe product or a rejected shipment. A minor issue is a small gap. For each finding, agree on a corrective action and a deadline. Follow up in the next audit. Keep audit records for at least 3 years. In Uganda, a maize exporter does monthly self-audits using a 2-page checklist. In CÃ´te d'Ivoire, a cocoa cooperative trains two farmers as auditors. They rotate so no one audits their own area. Internal audits help you improve continuously. They also show buyers you are serious about quality. Don't fear themâuse them to fix problems early.

lessons.title: Corrective actions when things go wrong
lessons.body: When something goes wrongâa rejected batch, a customer complaint, or an audit findingâyou need a corrective action. This is not just fixing the immediate problem; it's about stopping it from happening again. Follow a simple 5-step method: 1) Identify the problem clearly. 2) Find the root cause. 3) Decide on a corrective action. 4) Implement it. 5) Check if it worked. For example, if a shipment of dried fruit was rejected for too much moisture, don't just dry that batch longer. Ask why moisture was high. Maybe the dryer temperature was not checked. Root cause: no thermometer calibration. Corrective action: calibrate thermometers monthly and record it. Use a form to document each corrective action: date, problem, root cause, action taken, who responsible, deadline, and verification date. Keep these records. They show auditors you learn from mistakes. For customer complaints, respond within 48 hours. Thank them, investigate, and tell them what you will do. If a recall is needed, have a plan: who calls buyers, how you track affected batches, how you dispose of product. In South Africa, a juice exporter uses a simple corrective action log. In Egypt, a date processor uses a fishbone diagram (a simple cause-and-effect chart) to find root causes. Train your team to report problems without fear. A mistake hidden is a mistake repeated. Celebrate when someone finds and fixes a problem. That's how you build a culture of quality.

lessons.title: Preparing for ISO 9001 or HACCP certification
lessons.body: ISO 9001 and HACCP are international standards that can open export markets. ISO 9001 is about quality management; HACCP is about food safety. Many African exporters start with HACCP if they handle food, then add ISO 9001. Certification means an external auditor checks your system and gives you a certificate. It costs moneyâanywhere from $2,000 to $10,000 depending on your size and country. But it can pay off with bigger buyers. To prepare, first decide which standard you need. Ask your buyers. Then get a copy of the standard. You can buy from ISO.org or your national standards body (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, SON in Nigeria). Read the requirements. Compare them to your current system. Identify gaps. For HACCP, you must do a hazard analysis: list every step where food safety could go wrong (e.g., bacteria, chemicals, foreign objects). Then set critical control points (CCPs) and limits. For example, pasteurisation temperature must be at least 72Â°C for 15 seconds. Monitor and record. For ISO 9001, you need documented procedures for key processes, internal audits, corrective actions, and management review. Start by implementing your simple quality manual, document control, training, and internal audits. Run your system for at least 3 months before the certification audit. Collect records. Then contact a certification body (e.g., SGS, Bureau Veritas, or local firms). They will do a pre-assessment if you want. The main audit takes 1-3 days. If you pass, you get a certificate valid for 3 years, with annual surveillance audits. In Rwanda, a coffee cooperative got HACCP and increased exports to Europe. In Morocco, a canned fish exporter got ISO 9001 and now sells to Carrefour. It's a journey, but you can do it step by step.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a quality manual?
options: A) To impress buyers with a long document
B) To provide a rulebook for consistent production
C) To replace training for staff
D) To list all your customers
quiz.explanation: A quality manual documents how you make products consistently, serving as a daily reference.

quiz.q: How long should a quality manual be for a small African exporter?
quiz.explanation: A concise 10-15 page manual is practical and sufficient for small exporters.

quiz.q: What should you include in a quality manual?
options: B) Sections for key processes like buying, production, and shipping
C) A list of all employees' birthdays
quiz.explanation: The manual should cover each key process with what you do, who does it, and records kept.

quiz.q: Why is it important to number sections in a quality manual?
options: A) To make it look professional
B) To easily refer to them in training and audits
quiz.explanation: Numbering helps reference specific parts during training and audits.

quiz.q: What is document control?
options: A) Locking documents in a safe
B) Ensuring everyone uses the latest version of documents
C) Writing documents in secret code
quiz.explanation: Document control prevents use of outdated versions, ensuring consistency.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to code documents?
options: B) Use codes like QM-01, WI-01, FR-01
D) Use no codes at all
quiz.explanation: Unique codes like QM-01 help identify and track documents easily.

quiz.q: Who should be the document controller in a small team?
options: B) One designated person, even part-time
quiz.explanation: One person should be responsible for updating and distributing documents.

quiz.q: How should obsolete documents be marked?
options: B) Stamped 'OBSOLETE' and kept for records
D) Kept in a separate folder without marking
quiz.explanation: Obsolete documents should be clearly marked and retained for reference.

quiz.q: How long should batch records be kept?
options: C) At least 3 years or as buyer requires
quiz.explanation: Records are typically kept for 3 years to meet audit and buyer requirements.

quiz.q: What is a training matrix?
options: A) A table listing staff and required skills
quiz.explanation: A training matrix identifies who needs what training.

quiz.q: How long should training sessions be for small teams?
quiz.explanation: Short, regular sessions of about 30 minutes are effective and manageable.

quiz.q: What should you keep as proof of training?
options: B) A training record with date, topic, attendees, and test result
C) A photo of the trainer
quiz.explanation: A written record serves as evidence for audits.

quiz.q: How can you train low-literacy staff?
options: A) Give them a long manual
quiz.explanation: Visual aids help low-literacy staff understand critical steps.

quiz.q: What is an internal audit?
options: A) An audit by a buyer
B) A check-up on your own quality system
quiz.explanation: Internal audits are self-checks to find problems before external audits.

quiz.q: How often should you audit each part of your system?
options: B) At least once a year
quiz.explanation: Annual coverage of all areas ensures the system remains effective.

quiz.q: Who should conduct internal audits?
options: A) The person responsible for the area
B) Someone not auditing their own work
quiz.explanation: Auditors should be independent of the area being audited for objectivity.

quiz.q: What is a major audit finding?
options: B) Something that could cause unsafe product or rejected shipment
quiz.explanation: Major findings are serious issues that could lead to product failure or rejection.

quiz.q: What should you do after an internal audit finding?
options: B) Agree on a corrective action and deadline
D) Wait for the next audit
quiz.explanation: Corrective actions with deadlines ensure problems are fixed.

quiz.q: What is the first step in a corrective action?
quiz.explanation: Clearly defining the problem is the first step before finding root cause.

quiz.q: What is a root cause?
options: B) The underlying reason why a problem occurred
quiz.explanation: Root cause is the fundamental reason that, if fixed, prevents recurrence.

quiz.q: How soon should you respond to a customer complaint?
quiz.explanation: Prompt response shows you take complaints seriously and helps resolve issues quickly.

quiz.q: What is a fishbone diagram used for?
quiz.explanation: A fishbone diagram helps identify potential causes of a problem.

quiz.q: What is ISO 9001 about?
quiz.explanation: ISO 9001 sets requirements for a quality management system.

quiz.q: What is HACCP about?
quiz.explanation: HACCP is a systematic approach to food safety.

quiz.q: What is a critical control point (CCP) in HACCP?
options: A) A step where a hazard can be prevented, eliminated, or reduced to safe levels
B) A point where you control costs
C) A point where you check employee attendance
D) A point where you store finished goods
quiz.explanation: CCPs are specific steps in the process where control is essential to ensure food safety.

quiz.q: How long should you run your system before a certification audit?
quiz.explanation: Running the system for at least 3 months generates sufficient records for the audit.

quiz.q: How long is an ISO 9001 certificate valid?
options: B) 3 years with annual surveillance audits
quiz.explanation: Certificates are typically valid for 3 years, with annual audits to maintain certification.

quiz.q: What should you do first when preparing for certification?
options: A) Contact a certification body immediately
B) Decide which standard you need and get a copy
quiz.explanation: Understanding the standard and your needs is the first step before contacting certifiers.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of certification for African exporters?
options: B) It can open access to bigger buyers
D) It replaces the need for quality control
quiz.explanation: Certification demonstrates compliance and can attract international buyers.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to document corrective actions?
options: A) Use a form with date, problem, root cause, action, responsible, deadline, verification
quiz.explanation: A structured form ensures all steps are recorded and followed up.
